title: Room-temperature, electrically pumped laser grown in a silicon CMOS flow

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a laser whose light-producing semiconductor layers are grown on silicon and fabricated alongside CMOS transistors, with electrical power sustaining continuous laser emission at room temperature. The intended gain medium uses group-IV semiconductors, such as germanium–tin and silicon–germanium–tin, rather than transferred III–V semiconductor material. The target combines an operating capability—room-temperature continuous-wave electrical lasing—with a manufacturing capability: a qualified process that produces functioning lasers and transistors together.

GeSn and SiGeSn offer a route to optical gain because alloy composition and epitaxial strain can be selected to produce a direct bandgap, which favors light emission. This property is engineered; it does not apply automatically to every GeSn composition or strain state. A demonstrated cryogenic GeSn/SiGeSn laser supplies an experimental foundation, but the supplied evidence does not demonstrate the complete room-temperature, transistor-integrated platform.

significance.text: Silicon photonics already provides waveguides, modulators and photodetectors. Adding efficient coherent sources through a transistor-compatible group-IV growth and fabrication sequence could simplify integration and enable greater source density. The consequential advance would be the ability to manufacture light sources together with electronics without transferring III–V gain material. It would extend the scope of silicon manufacturing, rather than introduce the first laser on silicon or the first laser fabricated using wafer-level processing.

Existing heterogeneous InP-on-silicon lasers already support commercial pluggable optical transceivers for data centers and high-performance computing. They establish that integrated coherent sources have practical value and that heterogeneous manufacturing is a substantial existing baseline. A group-IV approach would therefore need to demonstrate benefits against a mature alternative; eliminating material transfer alone would not establish better cost, reliability or production scale.

System-level synthesis: dense sources could benefit optical interconnects, sensing and photonic processors if their wavelength, useful output, coupling, electrical consumption, heat load and reliability fit those applications. These are conditional downstream possibilities. A room-temperature laser by itself would not establish a low-energy optical link, a complete sensor or a useful photonic processor, and manufacturing compatibility would not by itself guarantee economic superiority.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central capability to establish is sustained, electrically pumped continuous-wave lasing at or above 300 K in a group-IV epitaxial structure, followed by its integration into a qualified CMOS transistor process. The documented 2024 device reaches pure continuous-wave operation only up to 35 K. Extending that demonstrated operating range to room temperature while maintaining useful optical output and electrical efficiency is a substantial unresolved step within the supplied evidence. Whether later work has already closed any part of that gap is not established by this record.

Engineering synthesis: the laser must sustain sufficient optical gain to overcome losses under continuous electrical injection, while managing the heat generated during operation. Composition and strain must support the required band structure, and the epitaxial stack, current-injection structure and optical cavity must work together over the intended temperature range. Direct-gap material design is therefore an enabling ingredient, rather than a complete solution to efficient room-temperature lasing.

Foundry integration is a separate barrier from achieving lasing in a nominally CMOS-compatible device. The peer-review material associated with the 2024 study raises practical concerns about introducing these lasers alongside front-end CMOS field-effect transistors. Actual co-integration must establish compatible processing temperatures, contamination controls and functioning transistors after fabrication. A device grown on a silicon wafer does not by itself demonstrate that manufacturing sequence.

The alternative III–V route illustrates why contamination control matters, but its limitations should be described precisely. Liang and Bowers's 2021 review reports that CMOS-compatible ohmic contacts had addressed the cited Au/Pt contact-metal constraint. It separately explains that III–V constituent elements can act as CMOS dopants, requiring dedicated processing tools and associated drainage and exhaust systems to avoid cross-contamination. This supports a manufacturing-integration challenge, not a claim that all III–V integration inevitably requires prohibited contact metals.

current_state.text: On 3 December 2024, Seidel, Liu, Concepción and colleagues reported an electrically pumped GeSn/SiGeSn multiple-quantum-well microdisk laser grown on a 200-mm silicon wafer in Nature Communications. The primary paper explicitly limits pure continuous-wave lasing to 35 K; higher-temperature lasing uses pulsed pumping. This demonstrates an electrically driven group-IV coherent source on silicon at cryogenic temperatures, rather than the proposed room-temperature CMOS platform.

The study's supplementary information reports a threshold of approximately 5 kA/cm², corresponding to about 4 mA, at 5 K for pulses ranging from 100 nanoseconds to a few microseconds. A 9 December 2024 institutional news release separately gives 5 mA at 2 V and describes operation up to 90 K without resolving the pumping conditions at that temperature. These figures must not be combined into a demonstrated continuous-wave operating point of 5 mA and 2 V at 90 K. The release's temperature statement could concern another pumping regime and does not establish a conflict between equivalent measurements.

The research notes cite a 2025 IEEE Silicon Photonics conference report as describing operation below 100 K. No text from that citation was retained in the supplied evidence, so its operating conditions and relationship to the 2024 result cannot be checked here. The citation therefore does not establish an additional temperature milestone or an updated continuous-wave limit in this record.

For comparison, Di Liang and John E. Bowers's 2021 review documents commercial heterogeneous InP-on-silicon lasers and an accelerated operating test involving 30 heterogeneous distributed-feedback lasers at 80 °C under elevated current. During the 23,500-hour test, less than 10% bias-current drift was needed to maintain 10 mW output. This is a useful reliability comparator, but it is not a field-lifetime measurement or a wafer-yield benchmark. The retained review extractions are truncated later in the document; the supplied evidence review identifies complete relevant passages supporting these particular observations.

The research notes also attribute field experience from more than 6 million heterogeneously integrated InP-on-silicon lasers and a failure rate of 0.05 FIT to a March 2025 SPIE report by Vallini and colleagues. The saved artifact contains no extractable text, so the report's identity, numerical claims and measurement scope could not be verified in the supplied review. These figures remain attributed research-note claims, rather than established benchmarks for this record; the extraction limitation is not evidence that they are false.

Evidence boundary: the supplied record establishes dated achievements and limitations, but contains no completed freshness review through 1 November 2026. It therefore cannot establish whether room-temperature electrically pumped group-IV lasing, or the full transistor-integrated target, remains undemonstrated on that date.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed optical demonstration: show continuous-wave, electrically pumped lasing at or above 300 K from a group-IV epitaxial stack on a standard silicon wafer. Report the operating temperature, pumping regime, threshold current and current density, electrical input, useful optical output and wall-plug efficiency under sustained operation. Set acceptable performance limits for a named integration application before evaluating success. The 300-K continuous-wave requirement and these reporting expectations are proposed completion criteria, not published consensus thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Group-IV-on-silicon epitaxy sustains continuous-wave electrical lasing at ≥300 K

completion_criteria.text: Proposed manufacturing demonstration: fabricate the laser alongside functioning CMOS transistors in a documented foundry process, with evidence that the combined sequence respects thermal budgets and contamination requirements. Measure transistor performance after the laser-processing steps and demonstrate the optical coupling required by the selected application. This would address the distinction between a CMOS-compatible laser structure and a qualified process for transistor co-integration.
completion_criteria.label: Qualified foundry process co-integrates lasers with functioning CMOS transistors

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and deployment demonstration: reproduce the result across multiple devices, wafer locations and fabrication runs, and preferably through independent replication. Characterize sustained output, temperature tolerance, degradation, application-appropriate lifetime and wafer yield. Compare against heterogeneous III–V-on-silicon alternatives under matched operating conditions; the documented 23,500-hour accelerated test offers context, but does not impose a mandatory threshold. Any cost or scale claim should be supported by production and economic evidence. Finite demonstrations establish performance across the tested devices and conditions, rather than universal compatibility with every CMOS process or photonic application.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible laser performance and deployment limits characterized across fabrication runs

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — OPT-09, Few-femtojoule optical links inside computing packages, has the closest application overlap: a co-integrated laser could supply light for such links. OPT-03 concerns the source and its manufacturing process, whereas OPT-09 concerns the energy and performance of a complete link. Laser efficiency, coupling losses and the rest of the link would determine whether this source helps meet that separate objective.

Roster-based synthesis — OPT-01, Cascadable few-photon optical transistor, concerns using light to control light and passing a usable signal between stages. OPT-02, Arrays of deterministic single-photon sources above the loss threshold, concerns controlled individual-photon generation and array performance. OPT-03 instead targets electrically sustained coherent laser emission and CMOS co-integration. A laser could support experiments or systems involving either concept, but does not establish optical transistor cascadability or deterministic single-photon emission.

Roster-based synthesis — OPT-10, Room-temperature short-wave-infrared photon-counting cameras, shares an interest in room-temperature optoelectronics, but addresses detection rather than coherent emission. OPT-05, Video-rate cellular imaging through living tissue, and OPT-06, Practical visible far-field super-resolution optic, concern imaging performance. An integrated source might be a component in an imaging system only if its wavelength and other properties fit; OPT-03 does not itself solve tissue-imaging or spatial-resolution limits.

Roster-based synthesis — OPT-07, Macroscopic programmable visible optical aperture, concerns controlling light across a large aperture, whereas OPT-03 concerns generating it within a semiconductor manufacturing flow. OPT-04, Laboratory-scale coherent hard X-ray source, also seeks coherent radiation, but in a different spectral and source regime; the proposed group-IV semiconductor laser does not establish hard X-ray generation. OPT-08, The quantum vacuum as a laboratory nonlinear optical medium, concerns a distinct light–vacuum interaction rather than semiconductor optical gain. These entries remain separate innovations despite their broad optical-engineering connections.

change_log.reason: The concept's identity depends on achieving the operating and manufacturing capabilities together.

change_log.reason: The earlier wording combined different pumping regimes and overstated the demonstrated continuous-wave temperature.

change_log.change: Retained the approximately 4-mA short-pulse threshold and the release's 5-mA, 2-V and 90-K figures with their respective measurement and attribution limits.
change_log.reason: Quantitative detail remains useful when it is not combined into an unsupported operating point.

change_log.change: Qualified the present-day absence claim and the 2025 conference summary.
change_log.reason: The freshness record is empty and the conference citation has no retained text.

change_log.change: Replaced blanket III–V contact-metal exclusion with the distinction between resolved contact-metal constraints and continuing constituent-element contamination controls.
change_log.reason: The 2021 review describes CMOS-compatible contacts while retaining dedicated-tool and waste-system requirements.

change_log.change: Identified the 2021 review authors as Di Liang and John E. Bowers and added its documented accelerated reliability test.
change_log.reason: The supplied review establishes the authors and provides a supported comparator with explicit test conditions.

change_log.change: Retained the more-than-6-million-device and 0.05-FIT figures only as unverified claims attributed to the research notes.
change_log.reason: The SPIE extraction cannot substantiate them, but an extraction failure does not justify declaring the claims false or erasing their provenance.

change_log.change: Reframed significance around group-IV epitaxy and transistor-compatible manufacturing, with conditional applications and separate economic validation.
change_log.reason: Commercial heterogeneous lasers already provide wafer-manufactured sources; room-temperature operation alone would not establish complete systems or cost superiority.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to cover measurable application performance, functioning transistors, reproducibility, lifetime and yield.
change_log.reason: These make the target assessable without inventing consensus thresholds or treating finite tests as universal proof.

change_log.change: Explained relationships to every other supplied roster entry as explicitly labeled synthesis.
change_log.reason: The roster supplies concept identities but no detailed evidence supporting stronger technical dependencies.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish the target's status through 1 November 2026; no present-day absence or achievement claim can be resolved from this record.
The 2025 IEEE conference report has no retained text, leaving its below-100-K statement, pumping regime and relationship to the 2024 device unresolved.
The institutional release does not specify how its 5-mA, 2-V and 90-K statements relate to one another or to the primary paper's pumping regimes.

The SPIE report's more-than-6-million-device and 0.05-FIT figures, including their measurement conditions and scope, remain unverified because the artifact has no extractable text. The review recommendation to remove these figures entirely was not adopted: they are preserved as explicitly attributed, unverified claims to retain useful research detail without treating it as established evidence.
The intended application, acceptable threshold and efficiency, useful output, wavelength, coupling requirements and thermal operating range have not been specified quantitatively.
A qualified transistor co-integration flow, reproducible wafer yield, application-appropriate lifetime and comparative manufacturing economics are not established by the supplied evidence.

brief.title: Lasers grown alongside the electronics on a chip
possible: Computers, sensors and chips that process information with light could have more light sources built into them. The goal is a laser grown directly on silicon alongside working transistors—the switches in electronic circuits—and powered continuously by electricity at room temperature.
why: Making lasers together with electronics could simplify chip manufacturing and fit more light sources into a small space. The light-producing layers would use silicon-family materials, such as germanium mixed with tin, without transferring separately made laser materials onto the chip.

sources.who: Lukas Seidel, Teren Liu, Omar Concepción and colleagues
sources.showed: They built an electrically powered laser from silicon, germanium and tin layers grown on silicon. It emitted continuously only at extremely low temperatures; warmer operation required pulses.
sources.quote: The electrically pumped microdisk laser operates from CW to short pulse conditions, at injection currents as small as 4 mA.
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates continuous, electrically powered laser emission from silicon-family materials grown on silicon.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate continuous operation at room temperature or fabrication alongside functioning transistors.

sources.who: Forschungszentrum Jülich, University of Stuttgart, IHP and CEA-Leti
sources.showed: The team described the same laser and reported operation up to 90 kelvin, an extremely low temperature. The release does not specify whether that limit applies to continuous emission or pulses.
sources.quote: For the first time, the researchers have demonstrated continuous-wave operation in an electrically pumped Group IV laser on silicon.
sources.cited_for: The release describes the team's laser and its intended route toward integration with silicon electronics.
sources.not_established: Its temperature claim does not establish continuous emission at that temperature or room-temperature operation.

sources.who: The silicon photonics conference report's authors
sources.showed: This is a conference report describing laser operation below 100 kelvin.
sources.cited_for: It concerns electrically powered silicon-family lasers operating at extremely low temperatures.
sources.not_established: It does not establish a higher continuous-operation temperature or room-temperature operation.

sources.showed: This is a report on field experience and reliability for indium-phosphide lasers integrated with silicon.
sources.cited_for: It concerns the reliability of an established alternative that combines separately made materials.
sources.not_established: It does not establish the reliability or manufacturing advantages of lasers grown from silicon-family materials.

sources.who: Di Liang and John E. Bowers
sources.showed: Their review describes commercial chips combining indium-phosphide lasers with silicon. It also documents an accelerated reliability test lasting 23,500 hours.
sources.cited_for: Existing integrated lasers provide a commercial and reliability benchmark for the proposed manufacturing approach.
sources.not_established: The accelerated test does not establish field lifetime, production yield or the performance of silicon-family lasers.

shown: Seidel, Liu, Concepción and colleagues built a silicon-grown laser powered by electricity. It sustained continuous emission up to 35 kelvin, far below room temperature. Higher-temperature operation used pulses, which reduce the heat load.
missing: The laser must sustain useful, efficient light output at room temperature under continuous electrical power.
A qualified manufacturing process must produce the lasers alongside working transistors without damaging them through heat or contamination.
Repeated fabrication runs must establish consistent performance, lifetime and the share of devices that work.

milestones.label: Silicon-grown lasers run continuously at room temperature
milestones.explanation: A laser grown from silicon-family materials on silicon would have to run continuously on electricity at or above 300 kelvin, meeting agreed application needs. This would establish the core operating capability.

milestones.label: Lasers and working transistors share a qualified manufacturing process
milestones.explanation: A qualified chip factory process would have to produce lasers and functioning transistors together, with light coupled into the intended circuit. This would establish manufacturing integration.

milestones.label: Repeated manufacturing runs establish performance and deployment limits
milestones.explanation: Devices across wafers and fabrication runs would have to show consistent output, temperature tolerance, lifetime and yield, with matched comparisons to existing lasers. This would establish practical deployment limits.

uncertain: The intended application and its acceptable power use, light output, wavelength and operating temperature range remain unspecified.
Whether growing the lasers with electronics would improve cost, reliability or manufacturing scale over established alternatives remains open.

page.title: CMOS-integrated room-temperature CW GeSn laser diode
page.definition: A germanium–tin (GeSn) laser, optionally using silicon–germanium–tin (SiGeSn) layers, grown on silicon in the same qualified fabrication flow as functioning complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) transistors. Direct current sustains continuous-wave emission—uninterrupted laser light—at an ambient temperature of at least 293 K.

goal.need: The 2–5 μm band contains molecular absorption features used for sensing. LASTSTEP targets a monolithic platform compatible with 200-mm CMOS processes. The electrical continuous-wave demonstration published on 3 December 2024 operates at cryogenic temperatures. Bonded III–V/silicon lasers already support manufactured transceivers; direct group-IV growth seeks another route to integrating light sources with electronics.

figures.caption: Accelerated operating test of heterogeneous 1310-nm III–V/silicon lasers.
figures.note: The stress current was twice the specified operating current; maintaining output required less than 10% bias-current drift.

statements.quote: a laser source with germanium tin alloys, operating under electrical injection up to room temperature.
statements.context: The project coordinator’s submission summary states the project objective.

statements.quote: offering a fully monolithic solution compatible with standard state-of-the-art 200mm CMOS manufacturing processes.

completion.title: A GeSn laser grown with CMOS transistors sustains continuous electrical lasing at 293 K.
completion.criterion: A GeSn/SiGeSn gain structure is grown and fabricated on the same silicon die as CMOS transistors in one foundry-qualified process. Without optical pumping, the laser sustains oscillation under direct-current injection at 100% duty cycle after thermal equilibration, with ambient temperature at least 293 K. Both devices function after the complete combined process; the transistors meet that process’s electrical acceptance specifications. The foundry qualifies the combined flow using its documented process-qualification tests.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis of the published laser-operation and monolithic-integration goals; no combined external acceptance test located.
completion.basis: Searched ITRS Outside System Connectivity, LASTSTEP and ELEGANTE objectives, and GeSn laser publications for a combined temperature/CW/transistor/process-qualification acceptance test; none was found. This test combines the published room-temperature CW electrical goal with monolithic CMOS integration. The 293 K convention follows Meyer et al.; transistor and process acceptance remain those of the named foundry.

milestones.title: An optically pumped GeSn cavity grown on silicon reaches laser oscillation.
milestones.criterion: A GeSn optical cavity grown on silicon reaches laser oscillation under optical pumping: an input–output threshold, spectral narrowing and a longitudinal cavity-mode pattern establish laser action. Wirths et al. demonstrated this in GeSn Fabry–Perot cavities, including a 1-mm-long waveguide, with lasing observed up to 90 K.
milestones.set_by: GeSn laser community; laser-action criteria applied by Wirths et al. in Nature Photonics (2015), and the demonstration recognised as a milestone by Seidel et al. (2024).
milestones.threshold_quote: a threshold in emitted intensity with increasing incident optical power

milestones.title: An optically pumped GeSn laser reaches room temperature.
milestones.criterion: An optically pumped GeSn gain structure reaches laser oscillation at room temperature; Meyer et al. explicitly use 293 K. Layers grown on silicon may be transferred to an insulating substrate for this milestone. On 21 January 2022, Bjelajac et al. reported a 5-μm-diameter microdisk lasing to 300 K under 880 kW/cm² optical excitation. On 8 July 2026, Meyer et al. reported an 8-μm-diameter GeSn multiple-quantum-well mesa laser at 293 K with a 500 kW/cm² threshold under 2-ns optical pumping.
milestones.set_by: GeSn laser community; Bjelajac et al., Optics Express (2022), explicitly identify room-temperature operation as a milestone. Meyer et al. (2026) use 293 K.
milestones.threshold_quote: An important milestone towards real-field applications is the ability to operate at room temperature (RT).

milestones.title: An electrically injected GeSn laser reaches a threshold at or below 10 kA/cm².
milestones.criterion: An electrically injected GeSn laser grown on silicon has a lasing threshold current density no higher than 10 kA/cm². ELEGANTE’s numerical target specifies neither temperature nor duty cycle, so this milestone does not establish room-temperature or continuous-wave operation. Zhou et al.’s peer-reviewed result reported a minimum threshold of 598 A/cm² at 10 K and pulsed electrical lasing up to 100 K, with emission near 2300 nm.
milestones.set_by: ANR-funded ELEGANTE project, submission summary; the numerical threshold target has no specified temperature or duty cycle.
milestones.threshold_quote: a target of 10 kA cm-2 for threshold

milestones.title: A GeSn laser grown on silicon sustains continuous electrical lasing at 100% duty cycle.
milestones.criterion: A GeSn/SiGeSn structure grown on silicon sustains laser oscillation under uninterrupted electrical injection, with 100% duty cycle; cryogenic cooling is allowed. On 3 December 2024, Seidel et al. reported this in a 5-μm-radius microdisk from a heterostructure grown on a 200-mm silicon wafer. Its continuous-wave threshold was 6.2 kA/cm² at 5 K, and pure continuous-wave operation stopped at 35 K.
milestones.set_by: GeSn laser community; Seidel et al., Nature Communications (2024), using multiple quantum wells (MQWs).
milestones.threshold_quote: Lasing in MQWs is achieved in the CW regime and any pulse width/frequency combination

milestones.title: A GeSn laser grown on silicon sustains continuous electrical lasing at room temperature.
milestones.criterion: A GeSn/SiGeSn gain structure epitaxially grown on silicon sustains laser oscillation under electrical injection at room temperature, without optical pumping, after thermal equilibration at 100% duty cycle. Room temperature is taken as 293 K following Meyer et al. This combines the temperature, electrical-injection and continuous-operation goals in the DFG-funded project. No matching experimental demonstration was found; the 2026 room-temperature quantum-well result uses optical pumping.
milestones.set_by: DFG-funded project 299480227, SiGeSn laser for silicon photonics, as stated in RWTH Aachen’s project summary; the 293 K convention follows Meyer et al. (2026).
milestones.threshold_quote: Current work targets a combination of these characteristics, towards a practical, continuously operated and electrically pumped room temperature laser.

not_found: No public foundry acceptance specification for GeSn lasers co-fabricated with functioning CMOS transistors was located.
No experimental report satisfying the combined completion test was found.
The supplied IEEE conference source, DOI 10.1109/SiPhotonics64386.2025.10985491, could not be opened.
The supplied EurekAlert release returned HTTP 403.
DFG’s GEPRIS page for grant 299480227 required JavaScript; RWTH Aachen’s project summary was accessible.

results.finding: One GeSn microdisk laser reached an electrical lasing threshold of 6.2 kA/cm².
results.detail: The threshold was measured under continuous-wave injection at 5 K; the heterostructure was grown on silicon.
results.quote:
For a 5-μm-radius microdisk, the lasing threshold decreases from 6.2 kA/cm
2
for CW lasing operation down to 5.8 kA/cm
2
for 1 ms pulses and 5 kA/cm
2
for 100 ns pump pulses.

results.finding: One electrically pumped GeSn microdisk sustained continuous-wave lasing up to 35 K.
results.detail: The GeSn/SiGeSn heterostructure was grown on a 200-mm silicon wafer.
results.quote: For the SiGeSn/GeSn MQW diode presented here, pure CW operation stops at 35 K.

results.finding: One electrically pumped GeSn microdisk sustained continuous-wave lasing up to 35 K.
results.detail: The continuous-wave operating limit was far below the 293 K room-temperature criterion.
results.quote: For the SiGeSn/GeSn MQW diode presented here, pure CW operation stops at 35 K.

results.finding: GeSn/SiGeSn laser on silicon achieved electrically pumped continuous-wave operation; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The release describes a ring-geometry laser grown on a silicon wafer. It does not state the continuous-wave temperature limit.
results.quote: For the first time, the researchers have demonstrated continuous-wave operation in an electrically pumped Group IV laser on silicon.

results.finding: GeSn/SiGeSn laser on silicon operated stably up to 90 K; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The release reports electrically pumped continuous-wave operation but says further optimization is needed to achieve room-temperature operation. It does not establish continuous-wave operation at 90 K.
results.quote: With its advanced multi-quantum well structure and ring geometry, the laser minimizes the power consumption and the heat generation, enabling stable operation up to 90 Kelvin (K) or minus 183.15 degrees Celsius (°C).

results.finding: One GeSn-on-silicon sample demonstrated optically pumped lasing up to 90 K.
results.detail: Fabry–Perot waveguides showed an intensity threshold, spectral narrowing and longitudinal modes. Pumping used 5 ns laser pulses; lasing at 90 K was observed at 1000 kW/cm² peak excitation.
results.quote:
At 1000 kW/cm 2 peak excitation, lasing 
was observed up to 90 K (inset of Figure 4a ).

results.finding: One optically pumped GeSn microdisk lased up to 305 K.
results.detail: The 15-μm-diameter microdisk was grown on silicon and transferred to an AlN pedestal. Pumping used 0.6-ns pulses at 50 kHz.
results.quote:
To conclude, we demonstrated lasing in a 17.2% GeSn microdisk
under optical pumping up to 305 K in strain free, underetched micro-
disks on pedestals.

results.finding: One optically pumped GeSn-on-insulator microdisk lased up to 300 K.
results.detail: The 5-μm-diameter microdisk was pumped at 880 kW/cm²; lasing was quenched at 303 K.
results.quote: Lasing is maintained up to 300 K and quenched at 303 K.

results.finding: One electrically injected GeSn laser on silicon reached a threshold of 0.756 kA/cm².
results.detail: The 80 µm-wide ridge device was measured at 77 K using pulsed electrical injection. The source is a preprint; the text does not establish peer review.
results.quote:
The maximum lasing temperature of 140 K and
low threshold of 0.756 kA/cm 2 at 77 K were achieved.

results.finding: One GeSn sample lased under optical pumping up to 90 K.
results.detail: Sample E was grown on Ge-buffered silicon. Lasing did not reach room temperature; the reported maximum was observed at a peak excitation of 1000 kW/cm².
results.quote:
At 1000 kW/cm 2 peak excitation, lasing 
was observed up to 90 K (inset of Figure 4a ).

results.finding: One GeSn microdisk grown on silicon showed optically pumped lasing up to 305 K.
results.detail: The paper reports an optical mode and a light-in–light-out threshold, but the supplied text does not establish spectral narrowing and a longitudinal cavity-mode pattern.
results.quote:
From 230 to 305 K, we clearly observe both the optical mode and
the nonlinearity of the L-L curve, which sets an upper lasing limit
between 305 and 308 K.

results.finding: One GeSn microdisk grown on silicon lased under optical pumping up to 305 K.
results.detail: The pump was pulsed and optical; the result does not demonstrate continuous electrical injection.
results.quote:
To conclude, we demonstrated lasing in a 17.2% GeSn microdisk
under optical pumping up to 305 K in strain free, underetched micro-
disks on pedestals.

results.finding: Optically pumped GeSn-on-insulator microdisk lasing reached 300 K; total sample size not reported.
results.detail: The GeSn was grown on silicon and subsequently bonded to a silicon wafer. The reported laser transition included an input–output threshold, linewidth narrowing and whispering-gallery cavity modes.
results.quote: Lasing is maintained up to 300 K and quenched at 303 K.

results.finding: GeSn-on-insulator microdisk lasing reached 300 K; total sample size not reported.
results.detail: The room-temperature result used pulsed optical excitation, not continuous electrical injection.
results.quote: Lasing is maintained up to 300 K and quenched at 303 K.

results.finding: Three GeSn/SiGeSn ridge lasers achieved electrical lasing at temperatures up to 140 K.
results.detail: The structures were grown on silicon. Lasing was measured with 700 ns electrical pulses at 1 kHz, a 0.07% duty cycle, rather than continuous injection.
results.quote:
The maximum lasing temperature of 140 K and
low threshold of 0.756 kA/cm 2 at 77 K were achieved.

results.finding: Three GeSn/SiGeSn ridge lasers achieved electrical lasing at temperatures up to 140 K.
results.detail: The structures were grown on silicon, but the maximum lasing temperature was below 293 K and the lasing measurements used pulsed electrical injection.
results.quote:
